## Q1: Using single-view image inputs

Single-view images are easily obtainable and very user-friendly, especially in real-world scenarios. Since our method is formulated as a probabilistic generative model, it can produce multiple 3D candidates that are consistent with the input image, producing plausible completion in unobserved regions, as shown in Fig.9 in the Appendix. 

## Q2: Robustness to potential transformer early mistakes

Our MCTS-guided sampling provides significant robustness to potential early mistakes. We evaluate this in the table below (and in Sec. A.4 of the appendix) by comparing the effect of initializing the first 21 tokens using ground truth. Our MCTS-based method demonstrates strong robustness compared with GT initialization, since it simulates the future outcomes of candidate next tokens, enabling assessment of their long-term impact rather than relying solely on local probabilities. This look-ahead mechanism effectively filters out potential early mistakes and prevents them from propagating through the generation process. More details have been updated in Sec. A.4 of the appendix.

| Category | Setting                         | CD ↓       | Topo-Sim ↑ | LPIPS ↓    | CLIP-Sim ↑ |
| -------- | ------------------------------- | ---------- | ---------- | ---------- | ---------- |
| Bridge   | a) w/o MCTS                     | 0.0238     | 0.987      | 0.0669     | 0.980      |
|          | b) w/o MCTS + GT initialization | 0.0194     | 0.989      | 0.0576     | 0.982      |
|          | c) w MCTS                       | 0.0168     | 0.998      | 0.0458     | 0.987      |
|          | d) w MCTS + GT initialization   | **0.0158** | **0.999**  | **0.0401** | **0.988**  |

## Q3: Dataset diversity

Our method can be extended to additional object classes that can be represented as procedural graphs, which encompasses a wide variety of object categories. For example, Infinigen alone provides >30 general object categories (e.g., plants, furniture, animals, etc.). We evaluated on cacti, trees, and bridges to cover various complex natural and man-made structures, and further evaluated on an additional fish category in Sec. A.2 to demonstrate our applicability to organic and non-hierarchical objects.

## Q4: Additional real samples

We have extended our real-world evaluation to show 20 more real image results in Fig. 6 of the main paper. From Fig. 6, our method successfully captures a broad variety of complex structures using our compact graph-based representation, demonstrating a strong generalization ability beyond synthetic data.

## Q5: Runtime

We provide a runtime analysis in our main paper (Sec.4.4 ) and supplemental (Sec. A.3), and have additionally updated the runtime measurements for real-world data. Note that our implementation is largely unoptimized for speed; we have now improved the search speed with better search parameters to accelerate our original runtime by 10x on tree category (with only a minor drop in LPIPS/CLIP from 0.081/0.977 to 0.086/0.976). 
We also provide average runtimes for the expanded set of real image data below. Note that often for real images, complex objects such as trees typically show strong occlusions (e.g., due to leaves), which can substantially reduce the search space for MCTS as it does not need to search to match many fine-grained branch details, resulting in faster runtimes for practical applications.

| Category        | w/o MCTS | w/ MCTS_fast |
| --------------- | -------- | ------------ |
| Real Cactus     | 9s       | 63s          |
| Real Leafy Tree | 41s      | 260s         |
| Real Bridge     | 21s      | 92s          |

## Q6: Bridge symmetry
While we do not explicitly impose symmetry constraints, this is encouraged to be learned in our prior. Our bridge tokenization loosely follows the design process for bridges (beginning from the center and sequencing one side of the bridge, followed by the other side), and the bridge training data is largely symmetric. This enables our autoregressive transformer to learn symmetric patterns without an explicit inductive bias toward symmetry.

summary.value: The paper proposes a framework to create 3D objects from a procedural graph representation. The graph generation is performed by a transformer model, trained to autoregressively predict edge-based tokens from a single image. At inference time, the approach uses Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) guided sampling. The model is evaluated on three procedurally generated categories – cacti, trees, and bridges – and outperforms strong baselines (TRELLIS, Wonder3D, TreeDFusion) on Chamfer Distance, Topo-Sim, LPIPS, and CLIP similarity.

strengths.value:
1. Using a transformer model to learn the procedural graph generation is interesting and allows more compact representation.
2. MCTS-guided sampling is novel and experimentally performs better for complex local geometry.
3. The approach seems to generalize for real images based on qualitative evaluations.

weaknesses.value:
1. The approach is limited to a single-view image which is not sufficient for capturing the full geometry of the object.
2. The overall generation will be limited by the limitations of autoregressive models, i.e., overall structure will be limited by the order of generation and errors can easily propagate. There is no discussion in the paper on the robustness of the generation process to small early mistakes.
3. The overall dataset is very limited with just three categories. The set of real-images is also very limited.
4. There’s no discussion of the runtime of the entire process. MCTS refinement is likely to add significant time to the overall generation process.

questions.value:
1. The bridge in the example is symmetric but there’s no inductive bias in the model. How is the autoregressive model learning symmetric structures?
2. How robust is the autoregressive generation to small error propagation?
3. What is the inference-time of the entire generation process?

## Q1: Relation to DI-PCG
DI-PCG assumes a fixed graph structure for each category it models, and predicts for each fixed graph the general object parameters. This makes it unsuitable for generating objects from categories with varying graph structures (e.g., trees, which typically contain different branching structures and thus graph topologies). In contrast, our method directly addresses this core challenge by using graph representations as a compact and flexible abstraction. This allows us to model highly complex and structurally diverse geometries (e.g., trees and bridges).

## Q2: Additional real-world examples
We have extended our real-world evaluation to show 20 more real-image results in Fig. 6 of the main paper. From Fig. 6, our method successfully captures a broad variety of complex structures using our compact graph‐based representation, demonstrating strong generalization ability beyond synthetic data.

## Q3: Scope of Objects
Our method can also be extended to model organic and non-hierarchical objects; we show additional results on the fish category in section A.2.

We also provide average runtimes for the expanded set of real image data below. Note that often for real images, complex objects such as trees typically show strong occlusions (e.g., due to leaves), which can substantially reduce the search space for MCTS as it does not need to search to match many fine-grained branch details, resulting in faster runtimes for practical applications.

## Q5: Interpretability of  generated graphs
Our graph representation is inherently interpretable, as it explicitly encodes the geometric skeleton (e.g., node positions) and shape attributes (e.g., branch radius, bridge semantic type, etc.). These generated parameters can then be directly edited by users. The procedural generator then produces updated geometry that faithfully reflects such user edits, enabling intuitive shape manipulation and controllable refinement.

## Q1: Training on a diverse set of objects

Generalized 3D models can be powerful from training on large-scale, diverse datasets. We believe a very interesting future direction would be to generalize our graph representation to unify a variety of categories, as many objects can be conceptually represented as graphs (e.g., not only procedural graphs but also skeleton graphs as commonly used in various production graphics applications). 

## Q2: Compare with the category-specific method
We thank the reviewer for suggesting the GET3D baseline. Our initial experiments in training GET3D on our tree data have shown noticeably worse quality generation than both TRELLIS and Wonder3D, as shown in Fig. 11 in the appendix; its triplane representation also struggles with finer geometric structures.

## Q3: Additional model/training details
Thanks; we’ve added more implementation details regarding our model and training in Sec. 4 in the main paper and Sec.A.6 in the appendix.

## Q4: Additional MCTS clarification
We are working to improve the clarity of our MCTS-guided sampling. In particular, a) Leaf states refer to states that contain no child states and have not yet been expanded in the search process. For example, at the beginning of each search round, the starting state—corresponding to the current partial graph—is a leaf state. b) Candidate child states are sampled from our transformer prior, conditioned on the currently generated partial graph of the state as the previous sequence. 3) $Q(s_i,s_{i+1})$ is defined as the average reward of state $s_{i+1}$, computed as the sum of the rewards (rendered mask similarities) of all its child states divided by the visit count of $s_{i+1}$.

We thank the reviewers for their insightful and positive feedback, for all recognizing our work as novel (9ktp,i7xi, G68W,w61D), and in particular highlighting that our neural procedural graphs offer a “compact” (9ktp, i7xi, G68W) and “conceptually elegant” (i7xi) representation. We are glad that the transformer design in our ProcGen3D was found to be “sound” (w61D) and the MCTS sampling scheme “improves image alignment” (i7xi, G68W) with “good qualitative results” (w61D).

summary.value: This paper introduces ProcGen3D, a novel framework for image-to-3D reconstruction that learns to generate procedural graph representations of 3D objects, rather than conventional voxel, point, or neural field outputs. Each object is represented as a procedural graph capturing topology, structure, and attributes that can later be decoded into high-fidelity 3D assets via traditional procedural generators. The authors employ a GPT-style transformer to autoregressively predict edge-based tokens conditioned on image features, and enhance alignment with input images through Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-guided sampling during inference. Experiments on synthetic datasets (trees, cacti, bridges) demonstrate superior results over diffusion- and transformer-based baselines such as TRELLIS, Wonder3D, and TreeDFusion.

strengths.value:
Innovative Representation:
The idea of learning procedural graphs as the latent 3D representation is novel and conceptually elegant. It bridges neural generative modeling and procedural graphics in a meaningful way.

Compact & Interpretable Outputs:
Procedural graphs are lightweight and structured, providing interpretable intermediate representations rather than opaque neural fields or dense meshes.

Effective Image Alignment:
The use of MCTS-guided sampling for test-time refinement is an original and well-motivated technique to improve consistency with image inputs without retraining.

weaknesses.value:
Missing comparison:
The paper doesn't compare to DI-PCG, which I believe is a very important, relevant baseline

Limited real world examples:
Although the method claims to generalize to real world examples, number of results for the same is limited.

Limited Scope of Objects:
The evaluated categories—trees, cacti, bridges—are all graph-structured and hierarchical. It’s unclear how well the method extends to more complex or amorphous shapes (e.g., vehicles, furniture).

Computational Overhead of MCTS:
While MCTS improves alignment, it introduces extra test-time computation, and runtime comparisons are not clearly reported.

questions.value: How interpretable are the learned graphs — can users manually edit them meaningfully?

summary.value:
TLDR: Neural procedural graph representation for image-to-3D reconstruction using transformer + MCTS-guided sampling.

This paper proposes ProcGen3D, which reconstructs 3D objects from RGB images by generating procedural graph abstractions (skeleton-like nodes/edges with attributes) that are decoded into high-fidelity meshes via pre-existing procedural generators. Uses edge-based tokenization + GPT-style transformer with MCTS-guided sampling for better image alignment. Key insight: predicting intermediate graph representation avoids issues with predicting raw parameters (usually non-differentiable). Evaluated on cacti, trees, and bridges using Infinigen and CEM generators.

strengths.value:
- Novel design choice: procedural graph as intermediate representation (skeleton-like abstraction) avoids non-differentiability issues of parameters.
- MCTS-guided sampling improves image alignment vs. pure autoregressive generation
- Compact representation (few hundred nodes for 10M+ face meshes)
- Well-motivated trade-off: parameters (unstable) vs programs (complex) vs graph (sweet spot)

weaknesses.value:
- Critical limitation: requires pre-existing procedural generators (Infinigen for trees/cacti, CEM for bridges) - cannot generalize to new categories without building generators first
- Cannot process organic shapes that are very hard to represent with procedural programs (animals, humans, irregular forms) - major applicability constraint
- Missing discussion with program-code-generation methods (LL3M, MeshCoder) that generate procedural code directly - should give more discussion on this.
- MCTS adds significant computational cost at inference time.
- Training only on synthetic data; real-world generalization not fully validated
- Procedural generators are external dependencies - not created or learned by the method

Thanks for your feedback. We are glad that you found our method to be both novel and well-motivated.

## Q1: Generalizing to categories without existing procedural generators

Existing procedural generators cover a wide variety of object categories, ranging from natural objects such as plants and animals to man-made structures like furniture, bridges, and cities. In Sec. A.2, we include results on an additional fish category to demonstrate our easy applicability to organic and non-hierarchical objects. For categories without existing procedural generators, our approach can be extended to model various other objects, such as graph-based parametric models, e.g., SMPL for humans, SMAL for quadruped animals, or MANO for hands. These models could also fit our graph abstraction (e.g.,  graph defining structural topology, nodes representing joint transformations, shape parameters encoded globally). This could enable our method to generalize beyond purely procedurally modeled assets to handle categories with even more diverse or organic structures.

## Q2: Relation to program-code-generation methods

We thank the reviewer for suggesting these LLM-based code-generation baselines and will include additional discussion in our final version. Since these methods rely on LLMs to directly produce program code, they are generally limited to relatively simple structures (limited amount of text/code that can be modeled) and struggle with more complex objects. As shown in Fig. 12 in our appendix, their performance degrades significantly on our complex categories. In practice, these methods typically generate only a few hundred lines of code, whereas our categories in Infinigen require many thousands of lines to fully capture the necessary structural and geometric complexity.

## Q3: MCTS Runtime

We provide a runtime analysis in our main paper (Sec.4.4 ) and supplemental (Sec. A.3), and have additionally updated the runtime measurements for real-world data. Note that our implementation is largely unoptimized for speed; we have now improved the search speed with better search parameters to accelerate our original runtime by 10x on tree category (with only a minor drop in LPIPS/CLIP from 0.081/0.977 to 0.086/0.976). 
We also provide average runtimes for the expanded set of real image data below. Note that often for real images, complex objects such as trees typically show strong occlusions (e.g., due to leaves), which can substantially reduce the search space for MCTS as it does not need to search to match many fine-grained branch details, resulting in faster runtimes for practical applications.

| --------------- | -------- | ------------ |

## Q4: Additional real-world examples

We have extended our real-world evaluation to show 20 more real-image results in Fig. 6 of the main paper. summary.value:
Reviewers acknowledge the novelty of using procedural graphs as an intermediate representation for image-to-3D reconstruction and find the overall technical design to be sound, with strong results on the evaluated categories. The MCTS-guided sampling strategy is viewed as a reasonable mechanism for improving image alignment.

Nevertheless, enthusiasm is tempered by several substantive concerns. The experimental scope is limited to a small number of graph-structured categories trained independently, raising questions about generality, scalability, and the fairness of comparisons to broadly trained baselines. Reviewers also note the significant test-time overhead introduced by MCTS, which was insufficiently analyzed in the initial submission. Additional concerns include reliance on pre-existing procedural generators, incomplete positioning against relevant alternatives (e.g., DI-PCG and program/code-based approaches), and clarity issues in the presentation, particularly regarding MCTS and experimental setup. Overall, while promising, the work leaves open questions about practical applicability and broader impact beyond the demonstrated settings.

reviewer_concerns.value:
**Addressed Concerns**

- Robustness of autoregressive generation / error propagation (Reviewer 9ktp):
The rebuttal provides quantitative evidence showing that MCTS mitigates early-token errors via look-ahead search (Appendix A.4).
- Runtime reporting and computational cost of MCTS (Reviewers 9ktp, i7xi, G68W):
The authors added explicit runtime analyses (Sec. 4.4, Appendix A.3), including real-image timings and a faster MCTS variant with minor quality trade-offs.
- Limited real-world examples (Reviewers 9ktp, i7xi, G68W):
Additional real-image reconstructions (20 more examples) were added, strengthening evidence of generalization beyond synthetic data.
- Clarity of MCTS formulation and training details (Reviewer w61D):
The rebuttal clarifies leaf states, child expansion, reward definition, and adds missing model/training details to the main paper and appendix.
- Missing citations to program/code-based shape representations (Reviewer G68W):
The authors added discussion of prior program-based shape generation methods in the related-work section.

**Outstanding Concerns**

- Limited category diversity and category-specific training (Reviewers w61D, i7xi, G68W):
While the authors argue extensibility and add a fish category, the method is still evaluated on a small number of hand-selected, graph-friendly classes, and does not demonstrate unified multi-category training.
- Dependence on pre-existing procedural generators (Reviewer G68W):
The method’s applicability remains constrained by the availability and design of external procedural models, which are neither learned nor constructed within the framework.
- Comparative positioning vs. alternative paradigms (Reviewers w61D, i7xi, G68W):
Although discussed, comparisons to DI-PCG, GET3D, and program-generation approaches remain indirect or limited, leaving some ambiguity about relative advantages in broader settings.
- Scalability to less structured or amorphous objects (Reviewers i7xi and G68W):
Extensions to organic or non-hierarchical shapes are argued conceptually, but empirical evidence remains limited.

summary.value: This paper proposes a new algorithm for 3D generation conditioned on an image prompt. Instead of NeRFs, SDFS, etc. it utilizes procedural graph abstractions as 3D representations. Those graph abstractions are then tokenized and a GPT-style Transformer is trained to do next-token prediction given a pre-trained image embedding. During inference time, the algorithm includes a Monte Carlo Tree Search sampling procedure to better enable the generation of fine details. Experiments are carried out on several categories of procedurally-generated objects, showing improvements over TRELLIS, Wonder3D, and TreeDFusion (on the tree category). The efficacy of the method is also validated on real-world images from those categories of objects.

strengths.value:
- As far as I know, this is the first work on image-conditioned 3D generation using procedural graphs as the 3D representation. Procedural graphs have many advantages, such as generality and being able to represent details well and succintly.
- The construction of the Transformer-based generative model is sound.
- Experiments show good qualitative results.

weaknesses.value:
The weaknesses of the paper fall into two main points. First, I think that the experiments are incomplete.
- The model is trained separately on each category of objects. This calls the experimental results' generality into question. Was training done on a more diverse dataset?
- Wonder3D and TRELLIS were both trained on a diverse set of objects. Therefore, comparing to them in a category-specific manner is not quite fair to them. It would strengthen the paper to include another category-specific baseline beyond TreeDFusion on trees - Get3D [1], for example?

Second, the presentation is unclear at some important points.
- No details of the model or training were provided in the appendix.
- The exposition of the MCTS is confusing at times. 1) How is a leaf state defined? 2) How are candidate child states computed? 3) How is $Q(s_i, s_{i+1})$ defined?

[1] Gao et al. "GET3D: A Generative Model of High Quality 3D Textured Shapes Learned from Images", NeurIPS 2022.
